title: Clue One: A Switch That Fires
blurb: Chicago, 1941 to 1959. A shy teenager and a doctor turn the nerve cell into an all-or-none switch, and switches into logic; but their nets cannot learn. The first candle is lit (THE BRAIN IS A LOGIC MACHINE), with a dissenter at its rim. Hebb and Turing guess where learning might live; Dartmouth names the field, and young Minsky, who had built a learning machine, turns to rules, and one young engineer never gets over it. A frog's eye puts the candle out after sixteen years.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: a parchment plate turns the 1943 paper into lanterns on threads: a wick that catches only past its threshold ring, then AND and OR lanterns filling their truth tables. The camera descends onto the desk, where a parchment plate (parchmentPlate) lies in the lamp's pool, its ink rules faint. Top left, the date stamp 'CHICAGO · 1943'. The 1943 paper's figure is redrawn in paper-cut: a single hanging paper lantern (paperLantern, the threshold unit) with two threads running into it from the left, each thread ending in a small input knot. Around the lantern's waist a cut-line ring is drawn in ink: the threshold, labelled θ. MECHANICS, in sync: on 'switch' the left input knot lights (value 1) and a bead of light travels its thread into the lantern; the lantern's inner glow rises to the ring but not past it: the wick does NOT catch (act stays 0, a faint ember). On 'All' the second knot lights too; two beads arrive together, the glow climbs past the cut-line ring, and the wick catches all at once, a full flame, no half-measures. On 'nothing' one input drops out and the flame snaps fully dark. A tiny tally under each lantern counts arriving signals (1, then 2). On 'logic' (the second half of L0204) the plate splits into two lanterns side by side with identical wiring: the left lantern's ring is cut high (θ = 2, labelled AND) and the right one's low (θ = 1, labelled OR). Four input patterns play in turn on both at once (00, 10, 01, 11) as small lit knots: the AND lantern lights only on 11; the OR lantern lights on 10, 01 and 11. These four patterns play briskly in the music-only hold after the line, each lit wick chiming, so the viewer can read the logic without words. A small truth table builds itself in ink beside each as the patterns play. No quote card on this plate (the 1943 abstract sentence moves to the end-credits sources card). On-screen text is held to two items besides the stamp: the threshold rule, and one shared caption under the pair, 'AND · θ = 2   ·   OR · θ = 1', with each half set directly beneath its own lantern. The θ glyph on each ring is drawn ink, part of the plate. Plain cut in: the camera's descent onto the desk continues the move from the study.

BOARD MAP (canonical, from the staging appendix; repeated word for word): the Case Board is a fixed grid of slots laid out as network columns by era, left to right: C1 (1943–1969) the far-left input column, C2 (1969–1997), C3 (2006–2017), C4 (2018–2023), and the output, the glowing chat box, at the far right; the case card WHO TAUGHT IT? hangs in slot K at the board's centre; the suspect cards S1 RULES, S2 KNOWLEDGE and S3 LEARNING hang in the left margin, top to bottom; the founding row F1–F2 runs beneath columns C3 and C4; the question-card thread runs along the board's top edge (slots Q1 to Q4, left to right), a low-chroma oxblood string (emberRed rim mixed about 60% into candleAmber) that glints only where the lamp's pool falls; the Wall of Forecasts hangs to the board's right, its slots W1 to W8 left to right (W1 Turing, W2 chess, W3 Rosenblatt 1961, W4 Florence 2012, W5 Coulom, W6 the 30-to-50-years slip in shadow, W7 Hinton 2017, W8 an empty pin until ch15). shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the hands strike the first match and light the first belief candle; a push into its flame finds McCulloch and Pitts facing it and Ralph Gerard at the rim with his dial. CAMERA: SHELF (low macro; the first candle lit), then the push into the flame onto the stage. The candle-clock, first use; establish the rules carefully. CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. Tilt down from the board to the long paper-cut shelf beneath it. The hands strike a match and light the first candle at the far left. Lettered on it in Special Elite small caps (a paraphrase, never in quotation marks): THE BRAIN IS A LOGIC MACHINE; its base tag reads '1943'; no sleeve yet, the flame on the top ring. On 'candle' the camera pushes into the flame (a quick push into its brightness, never through black, so the line is never spoken over a dark frame) and we arrive on the paper stage: the same candle, huge, stands on a dark stage floor and throws a round pool of amber light across it, haze hanging in the beam. The narration states the rule aloud here, and the picture follows it word by word: on 'held', in the pool, facing the flame, McCulloch and Pitts are revealed (the holders, the film's rule: believers stand in the light); just after 'held' (the rule's other half is shown, not said: doubters stand at the rim) the camera drifts to the edge of the pool, where the light fades into shadow, and finds it empty for a moment; on 'logic' the lettering on the huge candle catches the flame. In the pause after L0209 a row of anonymous figures in lab coats far back on L4 passes by outside the pool without turning their heads. On 'Gerard' a third figure (gerard: dignified, round glasses, suit) is revealed standing at the rim, half in shadow, facing OUT, his long shadow thrown across the floor away from the candle (the film's rule: whoever doubts stands at the edge). On 'dial' a small paper-cut dial appears beside his raised hand, its needle sweeping smoothly through every value; beside McCulloch a little toggle switch flicks between two positions. The two images sit side by side for a breath.

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: Dartmouth, summer 1956: the new name is chalked, Minsky turns from his learning machine to the board of symbols and rules, and young Widrow falls for the dream at the rim. CAMERA: Dartmouth, outside and in (era location; no study visit: the RULES emblem is chalked on Dartmouth's own board). Slow tint crossfade from the Wall's candleAmber (ch02-s05b) to duskRose (a mood change; this chapter has no lamp changes, only tint crossfades, so the film stays out of black). Exterior first: a white colonial college hall with a cupola, silhouetted against a rose dusk over a wide green, elms at the edges, fog low on the grass. Date stamp 'DARTMOUTH · SUMMER 1956'. The camera rises to the top-floor windows and passes inside: a long room, a big dictionary on a stand near a window, a long table with papers, a chalkboard, a typed proposal page pinned beside it (its numbered topics too small to read; one line faintly lit by the lantern's glow). Figures at the windows in silhouette: John McCarthy (mccarthy, glasses, late twenties) by the chalkboard; Minsky by the table. On 'name' McCarthy chalks two words on the board: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE; beside them, the pinned proposal page's dateline catches the light (the label notes the name came in the proposal of August 1955, before this summer). On 'Minsky' his name card rises; on 'learning', on the sill beside the lantern, a small paper-cut of the learning machine he had helped build at Harvard in 1951 (a rack of glowing tubes and a few knobs, SNARC) glows once, so the eye has what the ear is told. On 'symbols' Minsky turns his back on a small paper lantern hanging at the window and faces the chalkboard full of symbols and branching rules; the lantern swings gently, still lit. On 'suspect' (landing on 'Rules') the camera glances, for one beat, to a small paper-cut key over a branching tree chalked in the board's corner: the RULES suspect's emblem from the Case Board (ch01-s05), now with a face to it. On L0216 the camera finds, at the far end of the room by the door, a young man in jacket, tie and heavy glasses, Bernard Widrow (widrow), half in shadow, at the rim; his name card rises. On 'good' he looks not at the chalkboard but at the little swinging lantern Minsky turned from, and its light catches the rim of his glasses. On 'fell' his verbatim words rise beside him as a quote card (the card carries its date: he recalled it in 2005) and stay up through L0217 and the hold. On 'downhill' the lantern's swinging glow throws a faint misty-hill outline on the wall beside him, and a single bead of light rolls down its slope and settles in the valley: a first glimpse of the downhill landscape the film will return to. On 'Remember' the frame softly irises down on Widrow and the lantern together (an in-shot iris that never closes fully).

shots.visual: THIS SHOT: the frog's eye picks out features, the logic-machine candle goes out at sixteen rings, and back in the study the first clue is pinned and X-ray band 1 lights. CAMERA: stage, then the reverse flame push out to SHELF, a tilt up to BOARD (the C1 pin as an insert), then X-RAY (the column drawn square-on over the board). Palette crossfade back to the candle's paper stage (crossfadeMood duskRose to candleAmber, brief; never through black). CANDLE-CLOCK RULE (canonical; repeated word for word in every candle shot): every belief candle is cut to the same lit height, 45 scored rings at a pitch of 6 px per ring at L3 (270 px), its flame on the top ring and a small tag at its base giving the year it was lit. It burns down one ring per year the belief is held. The wax that burns away is never lost: it stays above the stub as a ghost paper sleeve, ring-scored and translucent in the haze, so sleeve plus stub is always the full lit height and the SLEEVE's length is the years (16 rings = 96 px; 39 rings = 234 px). The sleeves are the bars of the chart: a longer sleeve means a belief held longer. A candle still lit has a live flame where sleeve meets stub; one put out keeps its sleeve, dark, with a thread of smoke; one that guttered has a frayed rim. The great candle has burned low: its flame now sits sixteen rings down, a ghost sleeve of sixteen rings above it. In its light, a paper-cut frog sits on a lily pad at the front of the stage, in silhouette, its large eye lit by a rim of amber. Date stamp '1959'. On 'features' the frog's eye opens into a magnified inset (an in-frame iris): a fine paper-cut lattice of retina where many small cells light up in varied, overlapping clusters as a shadow passes, far richer than the single wick of the logic lantern from s02, which hangs small and plain beside it for comparison; on 'brain' a faint paper-cut outline of the frog's brain behind the eye stays dark while the retina's clusters already glow (the eye does the picking-out first); the paper's author card, with all four authors' names and the year, sits under the inset and stays up through L0220. On 'logic' the candle's flame gutters. On 'Sixteen' it goes out: a thread of smoke rises and curls through the haze, and the pool of light on the stage shrinks to nothing. McCulloch and Pitts are left in shadow; Pitts, the smaller figure, lowers his head (restraint: no other gesture). At the end of L0219, a REVERSE FLAME PUSH (no lamp change, never through black): the camera pulls back out of the dying wick's last ember and the huge stage candle becomes the small stub on the study shelf: the stub stands at the far left with its dark ghost sleeve of sixteen scored rings above it and a small tag, '1943–1959 · 16'. On 'name' the camera tilts up to the board and the hands pin the chapter's clue card in slot C1, the head of the far-left input column: a paper-cut lantern with a wick, date-stamped 1943. Then, without narration, a short X-ray beat inside the pause and hold. X-RAY COLUMN (canonical; defined here, read in ch12-s07): the chat box is drawn as a translucent stratigraphic column of seven faint, empty, unlabelled bands, stacked bottom to top, with one thin seam between the third and fourth bands that never lights (the hand-cut stencils' seam). Each X-ray beat in the film lights exactly one band, in order from the bottom: 1 threshold lanterns (1943), 2 adjustable knobs (1958), 3 hidden layers and a backward arrow (1986), 4 furnaces and a sea of text (2012), 5 threads (2017), 6 type sorts (2018), 7 shears (2022). Lit bands stay softly lit at every later appearance; unlit bands stay faint. Here, just after the line, the column is drawn for the first time, faint, over the board: seven empty bands. A moment later only band 1 at the bottom lights, a scatter of tiny threshold lanterns glowing (the one component of this chapter really present in a modern chat model), and stays lit through most of the hold. It fades before the cut. The oxblood question card still sways on its thread.
